chunks: "The way I think about it, a fast edge is a wave travelling down a transmission line, so every rule is about keeping that line uniform and giving the return current a clean path.
First, route over a solid reference plane, usually ground, and never across a split or slot in it, because the return current has to detour and you get a big loop and EMI.
Second, keep the impedance constant: one width, one layer where possible, controlled-impedance stackup from the fab.
Third, keep it short and direct with as few vias as I can, and when I do change layers I put a ground via right next to the signal via so the return current can follow.
No stubs, no T-junctions, so point-to-point, and bends are 45° or curved.
Then spacing: keep other signals at least three trace widths away to limit crosstalk, and give clocks even more room.
Match lengths on buses and differential pairs, in time, not just millimetres.
And terminate when the line is electrically long compared with the edge, series at the source or parallel at the load.
The one thing I'd add is that it all scales with rise time, not clock frequency.
A 10 megahertz clock with a 500 picoseconds edge needs this treatment; a 1 megahertz signal with a 50 nanoseconds edge doesn't."
